definition: A trade structured around the price difference between two related things (locations, products, or time periods) rather than a bet on overall market direction.
core_idea: By simultaneously buying one position and selling a related one, a spread trader isolates a specific price relationship and reduces exposure to broad market moves.
key_points: Directional trades bet on the whole market moving up or down; spread trades instead target relative-value differences between two securities.
Because natural gas prices are cyclical, spread trading is more common in gas markets than pure directional bets.
Spread trades are popular because they reduce a trader's exposure to overall market direction.
relationships: Parent concept for location spreads, heat rate trades, time spreads, and swing trades
trading_implications: Traders favor spreads to isolate a specific relationship (location, gas-vs-power, time, storage) instead of taking outright market risk.
caveats: Spread trades still carry risk — just a narrower, relationship-specific risk rather than zero risk.
